stories.title: John McCullough of Kennedy Wilson Multifamily Development: 5 Questions
stories.excerpt: Since joining Kennedy Wilson following the firm’s $347 million acquisition of Toll Brothers’ apartment living platform in 2025, John McCullough has been serving as president of the real estate investment company’s multifamily development group, where he oversees every aspect of the firm’s U.S. development business. Kennedy Wilson’s acquisition of Toll Brothers’ platform gave it general partner interests in 18 apartment and student housing properties, with assets under management of $2.2 billion. The firm also purchased a pipeline of 29 development sites in various stages of construction. Toll Brothers’ entire apartment living management team has transitioned over to Kennedy Wilson under the leadership of McCullough, who previously led apartment living operations at Toll Brothers. But McCullough’s real estate path wasn’t always laid out for him, as he started out in the U.S. Navy and then eventually hit his business stride at school in Boston. Commercial Observer caught up with McCullough last month to discuss his entry into real estate, the Toll Brothers acquisition, and his mission at Kennedy Wilson. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: How’d you get started in real estate? John McCullough: I got started in real estate in a roundabout way. I went to the United States Naval Academy for my undergrad, and graduated in 1994, and then served five years in what we would refer to as the surface navy. If I had stayed in the Navy long-term, I would have trained to be the captain of a ship. I served on two large aircraft carriers out in San Diego, and it was a great experience. It was a really good grounding in the fundamentals of leadership I was put into a lot of situations that were incredibly difficult as a 23- or 24-year-old, but I learned a lot from that. Then I got out of the Navy and I went to business school at Boston University, and it was during that time that I started thinking that real estate could be a really int
bullets: Kennedy Wilson acquired Toll Brothers' apartment platform for $347M in 2025, gaining 18 properties.
Pipeline of 29 development sites in various construction stages now under Kennedy Wilson control.
$2.2B in assets under management; entire Toll Brothers apartment team transitioned to Kennedy Wilson.
stories.summary: Kennedy Wilson completed a $347 million acquisition of Toll Brothers' multifamily platform in 2025, adding 18 apartment and student housing properties ($2.2B AUM) and a pipeline of 29 development sites. John McCullough, who led apartment operations at Toll Brothers, now serves as president of Kennedy Wilson's multifamily development group overseeing all U.S. development activity. The deal brings institutional scale and an active development pipeline to Kennedy Wilson's platform.
stories.impact: This consolidation signals continued capital deployment into multifamily by tier-one operators and reflects confidence in the asset class despite recent headwinds. Kennedy Wilson's absorption of Toll Brothers' pipeline and management team positions it to move quickly on 29 sites—watch for accelerated starts in Toll Brothers' target markets (likely Sun Belt, coastal metros) as Kennedy Wilson executes its playbook.

stories.title: Southern Land Company Hires Tony Marchbanks as Head of Homebuilding
stories.excerpt: Southern Land Company has made a leadership hire to spearhead single-family home development in three key states, Commercial Observer has learned. Tony Marchbanks has joined the firm as national president of homebuilding, in which he will focus not only on the U.S., but also focus particularly on Tennessee, Texas and Colorado, according to Southern Land. Marchbanks brings with him 30 years of real estate experience and most recently served as chief operating officer for Highland Homes, where he launched a building spree in the Houston market, producing 1,000 homes per year, Southern Land said. “Higher interest rates and lack of job growth all culminate into a lack of consumer confidence, so you have all three key contributors to a good homebuilding environment that are headwinds at this time,” Marchbanks told CO. “But for a company like Southern Land, it’s actually a huge opportunity because they have expansion plans, particularly into Texas, which is the largest new home market in the country,” Marchbanks said. “Most builders secured their lot supply three years ago, and now they have too many lots. So it’s an opportunity for a company like Southern Land to find and [invest] in communities they wouldn’t have been able to in a strong market.” Southern Land is currently developing four master-planned communities across 5,000 individual lots in its portfolio. Marchbanks will oversee the construction, purchasing, sales and architecture for those soon-to-be neighborhoods. Southern Land has been making some changes in recent months by launching its own mortgage lending division in May to augment its sales division and support its construction pipeline, CO reported at the time. Build-to-sell homes are not the only residential asset class Southern Land has been dabbling in either, as it builds multifamily properties in Las Vegas; Erie, Colo.; and just outside Austin, Tex. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Southern Land Company hires Tony Marchbanks, ex-Highland Homes COO, as national president of homebuilding.
Marchbanks built 1,000 homes/year in Houston; focus now on Tennessee, Texas, Colorado expansion.
Industry headwinds (high rates, weak job growth) create lot-supply opportunity for well-capitalized builders.
stories.summary: Southern Land Company appointed Tony Marchbanks, former COO of Highland Homes (which built 1,000 homes annually in Houston), as national president of homebuilding. Marchbanks will lead expansion in Tennessee, Texas, and Colorado. Despite near-term headwinds—elevated interest rates, sluggish job growth, and weak consumer confidence—Marchbanks noted that most competitors locked in lot supply three years ago and now carry excess inventory, creating a strategic opportunity for Southern Land's expansion plans.
stories.impact: This hire and strategy are largely irrelevant to multifamily development, but the underlying observation about competitor lot glut and capital constraints in single-family is worth noting: single-family builders' capital constraints may push land availability higher, and if multifamily developers are active in the same markets (TX, TN, CO), the competitive land landscape could shift in their favor as capital-constrained homebuilders offload or pause acquisitions.

stories.title: How Trent Johnson, Brian Landrum at Harbert Management Corp. Invest in Senior Housing
stories.excerpt: Trent Johnson and Brian Landrum are senior managing directors and co-heads of the seniors housing team at Harbert Management Corporation, an $8 billion alternatives asset management firm founded in 1993. The group has been investing in the seniors housing space for 15 years, raising a $210 million investment fund in 2016 and a $510 million investment fund for the space in 2020. The group is currently on its third fundraise, as they attempt to capitalize on the first wave of Baby Boomers turning 80-years-old in 2016. The duo sat down with Commercial Observer to discuss their careers, how the asset class has evolved, the present and future of the senior housing space, and where the best investment opportunities will be in an increasingly important asset class. (This conversation has been edited for length and clarity) Commercial Observer: How long have you been involved in the senior housing space? Trent Johnson: I started investing in the space in 2012, which is where I met Brian at Fortress Investment Group. I actually came from a legal background. I started out as a real estate lawyer, and then I spent a lot of years at an apartment investment and management company, which was a large multifamily REIT based out of Denver, Colo, Apartment Investment and Management Company. I was recruited away to start and lead a seniors housing platform in Dallas, which is where I joined forces with Brian, and we co-headed that office here in Dallas. Brian Landrum: I started investing in seniors housing in 2009 at a predecessor firm, Walton Street Capital, which was a diversified real estate private equity firm, and then in 2012, I joined forces with Trent in 2012 at Fortress Investment Group, which is where we began working together, and then ultimately, made a decision to join up at Harbert Management Corporation in 2015. bullets: Harbert Management's seniors housing team raised $510M fund in 2020; now on third fundraise.
Team investing since 2012; 15-year track record in seniors housing; first wave of Baby Boomers turned 80 in 2016.
$8B alternatives asset manager deploying capital into aging demographics and long-term demand tailwind.
stories.summary: Harbert Management Corporation, an $8 billion alternatives manager, has been investing in seniors housing for 15 years through dedicated funds ($210M in 2016, $510M in 2020) and is now executing a third fundraise. Senior managing directors Trent Johnson and Brian Landrum lead the effort, capitalizing on the first wave of Baby Boomers reaching age 80 (which began in 2016) and the multi-decade demographic demand tailwind for senior living.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily, but signals robust institutional capital competing for age-restricted assets. For multifamily developers, this underscores demographic pressure on independent seniors housing and reveals where large capital pools are chasing yield—developers targeting 55+ or active-adult communities face well-funded, specialized competitors with demographic conviction and long hold timelines.

stories.title: Sunday Summary: The Rent is Too Damn Low!
stories.excerpt: Back in 2010, Jimmy McMillan ran for governor of New York on a pretty straightforward platform: The rent was too damn high. McMillan said it again and again, and named his political party The Rent is Too Damn High Party. (McMillan’s presence on the debate stage garnered national attention and Matthew Yglesias even titled a slim book with the same name.) Sixteen years later, McMillan is still not wrong, in that the average monthly rent just hit $6,655 in Manhattan according to research from Corcoran Sunshine — which is 10 percent higher than it was a year ago. There are a number of solutions that the Mamdani administration have proffered, but one that has perhaps attracted the most attention has been freezing rents on rent-stabilized apartments. In June, the Rent Guidelines Board issued a freeze on one- and two-year leases, which will certainly be popular with rent-stabilized voters. But one has to wonder if it will actually address the larger issue of affordability — especially if landlords begin to lose more money than they make on stabilized units. Some landlords are keeping units off the market rather than getting them in rentable shape. “Some of [the rent-stabilized units] require more work than others, but for the ones that need significant work — and I mean baseline, just to get them up to livable standards — we’re talking $30,000 minimum,” said Jose Tur, who owns two stabilized buildings in Washington Heights and testified before the RGB before their vote. In addition to the baseline, Tur told Commercial Observer that he would probably have to include another $30,000 per unit for the cosmetic fixes. And that’s on the lower end of the renovation spectrum. Matthew Engel, president of Langsam Property Services, says he has units that require $80,000 to $100,000 worth of work, and rent as low as $600 per month. “There’s no way for me to finance that work,” said Engel. “No bank would lend me $100,000 if I’m only going to be able to collect $6,000 a year in rent.”
bullets: Manhattan average rent hits $6,655/month, up 10% YoY; rent-stabilized units frozen by Rent Guidelines Board in June.
Rent Guidelines Board issued freeze on one- and two-year stabilized leases under Mamdani administration.
Risk: stabilized-unit economics deteriorate if landlords lose money; units may be removed from market.
stories.summary: Manhattan rents reached $6,655 per month on average, a 10 percent year-over-year increase, driven by persistent supply-demand imbalance. In response, New York's Rent Guidelines Board froze rents on one- and two-year stabilized leases in June. However, affordability concerns remain unresolved, and the freeze risks exacerbating owner economics on stabilized units, potentially pushing landlords to remove units from the market rather than accept below-market rents.
stories.impact: For multifamily developers in NYC, rent freezes on stabilized stock reduce effective competition in the market-rate segment—stabilized units drift further underwater economically, accelerating removals from the rental pool and tightening net-available supply. This reinforces strong fundamentals for new market-rate supply, especially in outer boroughs where stabilization requirements may be lighter; however, regulatory risk remains high and could depress development feasibility if rent caps expand to new buildings or stabilization thresholds shift.

stories.title: AI-Native Hanover Park Leases Full Floor at 387 Park Ave. South
stories.excerpt: A new lease with AI-native fund administrator Hanover Park and the expansion and extension of PMG Worldwide’s existing space have been recent highlights at TF Cornerstone’s 387 Park Ave. South, which has seen more than 100,000 square feet of leasing activity in the past year. The recent transactions follow K Health’s long-term renewal and the expansion of another TAMI user completed in late 2025. Hanover Park signed a lease for the building’s entire 10th floor, totaling approximately 19,269 square feet. PMG Worldwide renewed its lease on the entire second floor while expanding into the entire third floor, bringing its total footprint to approximately 38,744 square feet. “We’re pleased to welcome Hanover Park to 387 Park Avenue South and to expand our relationship with PMG Worldwide,” said Joe Lanzilotta, Director, Commercial Asset Management at TF Cornerstone. “The property continues to outperform the market as a destination for growing businesses.” The post AI-Native Hanover Park Leases Full Floor at 387 Park Ave. South appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Hanover Park (AI-native fund admin) leases full floor at 387 Park Ave South, 19,269 SF.
PMG Worldwide expands from entire 2nd floor to 2nd + 3rd floor, total 38,744 SF.
TF Cornerstone property logs 100K+ SF leasing activity in past year; outperforming market.
stories.summary: TF Cornerstone's 387 Park Avenue South has recorded over 100,000 square feet of leasing activity in the past year, including a full-floor lease (10th floor, 19,269 SF) to AI-native fund administrator Hanover Park and a renewal-plus-expansion from PMG Worldwide (expanding from 2nd floor to 2nd and 3rd floors, totaling 38,744 SF). The building continues to attract growing companies and technology users.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily. However, the presence of AI-native firms and tech-focused tenants in NYC office signals continued tenant demand in pockets of the market; this could correlate with job-growth tailwinds in specific Manhattan submarkets and translate to stronger renter demand nearby. For developers, sustained office leasing in trophy locations (Park Ave South) suggests that selective NYC office markets are not in distress—residential demand in surrounding areas should remain resilient.

stories.title: PMB, Loma Linda University Health Break Ground on Inpatient Rehab Hospital
stories.excerpt: PMB, a leading healthcare real estate developer, and Loma Linda University Health with Lifepoint Rehabilitation, a business unit of Lifepoint Health, recently broke ground on a new, 99,000-square-foot, 80-bed inpatient rehabilitation hospital in Redlands. Located at 11207 New Jersey., the three-story facility will function as a standalone hospital. “Breaking ground today represents far more than just laying the foundation for a new building – it’s a promise to the community,” said Nolan Weinberg, SVP of Development for PMB. “Inpatient rehabilitation is a critical bridge between acute medical recovery and returning to everyday life..” Loma Linda University Rehabilitation Hospital will be jointly operated by Loma Linda University Health and Lifepoint Rehabilitation. A summer 2028 opening is expected. Upon completion, Loma Linda University Health will transition its existing inpatient rehabilitation unit to the new facility. PMB’s partners on the project include general contractor Layton Construction, architect Material Design Architects and financing partner Harrison Street Asset Management. The post PMB, Loma Linda University Health Break Ground on Inpatient Rehab Hospital appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: PMB and Loma Linda University Health break ground on 99,000 SF, 80-bed inpatient rehab hospital in Redlands, CA.
Summer 2028 opening; jointly operated by Loma Linda Health and Lifepoint Rehabilitation.
Healthcare real estate development; financed by Harrison Street; general contractor Layton Construction.
stories.summary: PMB and Loma Linda University Health broke ground on a new 99,000-square-foot, 80-bed inpatient rehabilitation hospital in Redlands, California. Scheduled to open in summer 2028 and jointly operated by Loma Linda University Health and Lifepoint Rehabilitation, the three-story standalone facility will replace an existing inpatient rehabilitation unit. Harrison Street Asset Management provided financing; Layton Construction serves as general contractor.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily development. Healthcare real estate (senior housing and rehab facilities) is a distinct asset class. However, for multifamily developers active in the Inland Empire/San Bernardino County, note that major healthcare infrastructure investment signals job growth and population inflows that could support residential demand; monitor whether Loma Linda's expansion correlates with migration or employment growth in the region.

stories.title: Astoria Favorite :3Coffee Roasters Expands to Halletts Point
stories.excerpt: The Durst Organization has signed :3Coffee Roasters to a 1,232-square-foot lease for a new retail location at 30 Halletts Point in Astoria, Queens. Expected to open later this year, the new shop marks an expansion for the family-owned business and its second Astoria location. It will also be the first retail at 20 and 30 Halletts Point, which opened last year with 647 apartments. “Halletts Point is a thriving community with spectacular views of Manhattan and Queens. As the neighborhood continues to grow, we are selecting retailers that will bring additional value to residents and neighbors alike, and we are excited to welcome :3Coffee Roasters,” said Jody Durst, president of The Durst Organization. :3Coffee Roasters was founded by Astoria residents Fabian Guzman and Andrea Gomez. The brand first opened on Steinway Street in Astoria and later expanded to the Flatiron District in Manhattan, building a following for their neighborhood-oriented approach and high-quality offerings. The Durst Organization was represented in-house by Karen Rose and Eric Engelhardt and by KSR’s Zach Nathan, Mark Gallucci, and Hunter Lazan. :3Coffee Roasters was represented by Genaro Otero at Sinvin. The post Astoria Favorite :3Coffee Roasters Expands to Halletts Point appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: :3Coffee Roasters signs 1,232 SF lease at 30 Halletts Point, Astoria, Queens; second location for brand.
Halletts Point delivered 647 apartments in 2026; first retail tenant at property.
Family-owned coffee brand expanded from Steinway Street (Astoria) original to Flatiron, now back to neighborhood.
stories.summary: The Durst Organization signed :3Coffee Roasters to a 1,232-square-foot retail lease at 30 Halletts Point in Astoria, Queens. The coffee roaster's new location, opening later in 2026, marks the family-owned brand's second Astoria location (after its original Steinway Street store) and is the first retail at the residential building, which opened last year with 647 apartments. The lease underscores retail activation at the mixed-use property.
stories.impact: This is a retail story, not core multifamily, but it signals healthy retail demand and neighborhood vibrancy at a newly completed residential community in Queens. For multifamily developers, successful ground-floor retail activation at Halletts Point validates the neighborhood's food-and-beverage appeal and supports renter-friendly positioning; the brand's return to Astoria suggests demographic stability and local economic momentum in LIC/Astoria submarkets—positive indicator for rent growth and retention in nearby multifamily.

stories.title: CBRE Arranges Debt on Advanced Manufacturing Campus in San Jose’s Golden Triangle
stories.excerpt: CBRE announced it arranged $67.4 million in financing for Forge North First, a mixed-phase industrial/R&D campus and advanced manufacturing development in San Jose’s Golden Triangle submarket. Mike Walker, Brad Zampa and Andy Gross of CBRE’s Debt & Structured Finance team in San Francisco arranged the five-year bridge loan with floating-rate, non-recourse financing from an institutional lender on behalf of Four Corners Properties and a West Coast-based institutional investor. “The combination of surging occupier demand and extremely limited supply positions Four Corners to create significant value at Forge North First,” said Zampa. Four Corners, an established local investor and developer founded in 2005, has invested in 50 buildings totaling 7.2 million square feet. In January 2026, Four Corners and its institutional partner acquired the existing 205,800-square-foot, five-building campus from BXP. The mixed-phase program includes comprehensive modernization of the existing campus and development of two advanced manufacturing buildings totaling approximately 239,000 square feet. Four Corners Properties and institutional partner acquired 205,800 SF, five-building campus from BXP in January 2026.

Four Corners Properties and an institutional investor acquired the existing 205,800-square-foot, five-building campus from BXP in January 2026. The mixed-phase development program includes comprehensive modernization and two new advanced manufacturing buildings totaling approximately 239,000 square feet.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily, but signals strong institutional investment and capital availability for industrial/manufacturing real estate in the Bay Area. For multifamily developers in San Jose or Silicon Valley, robust demand for advanced manufacturing space and class-A industrial assets indicates sustained job growth and employer investment in the region—this supports residential demand and rent growth, particularly for workforce housing near tech and manufacturing corridors.

stories.title: Marcus & Millichap Closes Sale of Downtown Westfield Mixed-Use
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap arranged the sale of 251 North Ave. W., a mixed-use property in Westfield, NJ, for $5,260,000. Alan Cafiero, David Cafiero and Damien Rance of Marcus & Millichap exclusively marketed the property on behalf of the seller and procured the private buyer. “Downtown Westfield continues to be one of the most desirable mixed-use investment markets in New Jersey,” said Alan Cafiero, senior managing director investments in Marcus & Millichap’s New Jersey office. “The combination of a premier downtown location, immediate proximity to the train station and a strong, diverse tenant roster generated significant investor interest in this asset.” The property is a three-story, 17,831-square-foot building on a 0.18-acre lot with direct access to municipal commuter parking. It has nine suites and was renovated in 2014. The rent roll features a diverse mix of service-oriented tenants, including Columbia Bank, Edward Jones, the State of New Jersey, BAYADA Home Health Care and Rooster Spin. The post Marcus & Millichap Closes Sale of Downtown Westfield Mixed-Use appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Marcus & Millichap closes $5.26M sale of mixed-use property in Downtown Westfield, NJ; 17,831 SF, 9 suites.
Three-story, renovated 2014; diverse tenants include Columbia Bank, Edward Jones, State of NJ, BAYADA Home Health.
Location near commuter train station and municipal parking attracts investment interest; strong mixed-use market fundamentals.
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of 251 North Avenue West, a mixed-use property in Downtown Westfield, New Jersey, for $5.26 million. The three-story, 17,831-square-foot building on 0.18 acres features nine suites, direct access to municipal commuter parking, and a 2014 renovation. The diverse tenant roster includes Columbia Bank, Edward Jones, State of New Jersey, and BAYADA Home Health Care, demonstrating strong market fundamentals in a premier downtown location near the commuter rail station.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development. However, strong mixed-use investment activity in Downtown Westfield (NJ Transit proximity, diverse service tenants, $5M+ transaction) signals healthy suburban commercial real estate and ongoing demand for convenient, transit-accessible mixed-use properties. For multifamily developers, this underscores the viability of mixed-use development in strong commuter-rail suburbs and suggests rental demand from professionals working in NYC or North Jersey—targeting mixed-use or transit-adjacent multifamily in Westfield-caliber markets remains attractive.

stories.title: Nuveen Green Capital Closes $281M Record C-PACE Loan for Boston Condos
stories.excerpt: The steady climb of commercial property assessed clean energy (C-PACE) financing around the U.S. has made its way to one of Boston’s tallest buildings. Millennium Partners has secured a $281 million C-PACE loan to implement energy efficiency upgrades at the 62-story Winthrop Center in Downtown Boston, the developer announced Friday afternoon. Nuveen Green Capital originated the fixed-rate loan under the Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) Massachusetts program which marked the largest C-PACE financing to date in the New England region, according to the lender. The condo inventory of the roughly 800,000 square-foot mixed-use building completed in 2023 attracted strong lender competition with many debt funds chasing the loan, according to a source familiar with the transaction. The C-PACE debt closed concurrently with a $575 million commercial mortgage backed securities (CMBS) loan led by Morgan Stanley for the office and retail portion of the tower according to a presale report from Moody’s. CoStar first reported the MP Trust 2026-WTRP single-asset-single-borrower deal for Boston’s largest building in the city’s financial district. The combined $856 million debt package takes out a prior construction loan from Cale Street in October 2020 after the London firm stepped in following another bank who backed out during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, according to sources. “We were honored to partner with MassDevelopment to recapitalize the largest C-PACE-financed project in New England, one that has helped reshape downtown Boston with state-of-the-art, energy-efficient residences,” Mike Doty, senior director of originations for NGC, said in a statement. Christopher Jeffries, founder of Millennium Partners, said in a statement that the C-PACE loan “recognizes the investments we have made in energy efficiency while providing long-term capital that supports the building’s enduring performance.” The PACE Massachusetts program was updated in June 2026
bullets: Nuveen Green Capital closes $281M C-PACE loan for Millennium Partners' Winthrop Center, Downtown Boston; largest New England PACE to date.
Winthrop Center: 62-story, 800,000 SF mixed-use condo building completed 2023; energy efficiency retrofit project.
C-PACE loan closed concurrent with $575M CMBS loan led by Morgan Stanley for office component.
stories.summary: Nuveen Green Capital originated a $281 million C-PACE (Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy) loan for Millennium Partners' Winthrop Center, a 62-story, 800,000-square-foot mixed-use building in Downtown Boston completed in 2023. The fixed-rate loan, the largest PACE financing in New England to date, will fund energy efficiency upgrades to the condo-dominant asset. The PACE loan closed concurrently with a $575 million CMBS loan from Morgan Stanley for the office component.
stories.impact: Tangential to multifamily, but relevant for capital structure strategy. The dual financing structure (C-PACE for condo/common areas + CMBS for office) reflects lender appetite for green financing and mixed-use assets; it demonstrates that condo-heavy residential mixed-use buildings can access non-traditional debt sources. For multifamily developers considering mixed-use projects with condo sales or common-area energy-efficiency goals, PACE financing offers an additional capital tool to improve project economics and attract value-add lenders, especially in Northeast markets with established PACE programs.
